873: From pyruvate to the Krebs cycle
874: Nine steps in the matrix: pyruvate is fully oxidised to CO₂, and its electrons are loaded onto NAD⁺ and FAD.
875: Tally for one acetyl-CoA: 2 CO₂, 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP. The reduced coenzymes carry their electrons to the respiratory chain: ≈ 10 ATP.
876: Pyruvate coming from the cytosol loses one carbon as CO₂. The two remaining carbons are attached to coenzyme A: this is acetyl-CoA, the fuel of the cycle.
877: A complex of three enzymes: E1 (thiamine pyrophosphate) decarboxylates, E2 (lipoamide) transfers the acetyl to CoA, E3 (FAD) re-oxidises lipoamide and reduces NAD⁺. Irreversible; slowed by phosphorylation of E1 (PDH kinase) when ATP, NADH and acetyl-CoA are plentiful.
878: Which E1 cofactor carries the decarboxylated intermediate?
883: The acetyl (2 carbons) is joined to oxaloacetate (4 carbons): citrate, with 6 carbons, is born. Coenzyme A leaves free.
884: Aldol condensation, then hydrolysis of the citryl-CoA thioester, which pulls the reaction (ΔG°′ ≈ −31 kJ/mol). The enzyme first binds oxaloacetate, which creates the acetyl-CoA site (induced fit). Inhibited by citrate, NADH and succinyl-CoA.
889: The –OH group of citrate is moved by one carbon: citrate becomes isocitrate, ready to be oxidised.
890: Dehydration to cis-aconitate then rehydration, on a [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur cluster one iron of which binds the substrate. In the cytosol, aconitase that loses its cluster becomes IRP1 and controls the translation of ferritin and TfR1. Fluorocitrate blocks it.
896: First oxidation: isocitrate gives two electrons to NAD⁺ and loses one carbon (CO₂). What remains is α-ketoglutarate, with 5 carbons.
897: IDH3, NAD⁺-dependent: oxidation of the alcohol to a ketone (enzyme-bound oxalosuccinate), then decarboxylation, with Mn²⁺ or Mg²⁺. Rate-limiting step, activated by ADP and Ca²⁺. The NADP⁺-dependent IDH1/2 forms, mutated in gliomas and leukaemias, produce 2-hydroxyglutarate.
903: Second decarboxylation: another CO₂ leaves, another NADH is formed, and the 4 remaining carbons are linked to coenzyme A.
904: A complex built like pyruvate dehydrogenase: E1 (TPP), E2 (lipoamide), E3 (FAD, shared). The two CO₂ released in this turn come from the starting oxaloacetate, not from the acetyl that has just entered. Succinyl-CoA is also the starting point of haem.
905: Where do the two CO₂ released during one turn come from?
907: From the acetyl that has just entered
910: The energy of the bond to coenzyme A is used to make a GTP directly, equivalent to one ATP. Succinate is released.
911: The only substrate-level phosphorylation of the cycle: phosphate replaces CoA (succinyl-phosphate), moves onto a histidine of the enzyme, then onto GDP (SUCLG2 isoform) or ADP (SUCLA2).
912: Which residue of the enzyme is transiently phosphorylated?
917: Succinate loses two hydrogens, captured by FAD: a double bond appears (fumarate). This enzyme is also complex II of the respiratory chain.
918: Anchored in the inner membrane: covalently bound FAD (SDHA), three iron-sulfur clusters (SDHB), then ubiquinone (SDHC/SDHD). It pumps no protons. Inhibited by malonate; its mutations cause paragangliomas.
920: Oxidising a C–C bond is not exergonic enough to reduce NAD⁺
923: A water molecule is added across the double bond: fumarate becomes malate.
924: Stereospecific addition: only L-malate is formed. Fumarase deficiency predisposes to leiomyomas and kidney cancers; the accumulated fumarate inhibits α-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases.
925: What type of reaction does fumarase catalyse?
930: Last oxidation: malate gives back oxaloacetate, ready for another turn, and a third NADH.
931: A very unfavourable reaction (ΔG°′ ≈ +30 kJ/mol), pulled by the immediate use of oxaloacetate by citrate synthase.
932: How many NADH does one turn of the cycle produce?
934: In the inner membrane: electrons from NADH and FADH₂ flow down to oxygen; the energy released pumps protons, whose return makes ATP.
935: Per NADH: 10 H⁺ pumped (4 + 4 + 2), i.e. ≈ 2.5 ATP; per FADH₂: 6 H⁺, ≈ 1.5 ATP.
937: NADH gives its two electrons to ubiquinone. The energy released is used to pump four protons out of the matrix.
938: NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase, 45 subunits: FMN, then a chain of iron-sulfur clusters to the ubiquinone site; the conformational change spreads to the membrane arm, which translocates 4 H⁺. Inhibited by rotenone. A major site of superoxide production.
939: Which group first accepts the electrons of NADH?
944: The electrons of FADH₂ also join ubiquinone, but without proton pumping: they will yield less ATP.
945: Complex II is the succinate dehydrogenase of the Krebs cycle. Other FAD dehydrogenases also reduce ubiquinone: ETF-QO (β-oxidation), mitochondrial glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, dihydroorotate dehydrogenase.
946: How many protons does complex II pump?
948: Ubiquinol passes its electrons, one at a time, to two cytochromes c. Four protons are released on the outer side.
949: Q cycle of the bc1 complex: at the Qo site, one electron of QH₂ goes to the Rieske protein, cytochrome c1 then cytochrome c; the other crosses haems bL and bH and reduces a quinone at the Qi site. Inhibited by antimycin A.
950: Why is a Q cycle needed?
951: QH₂ carries two electrons, cytochrome c only one
955: Four cytochromes c deliver their electrons to the oxygen we breathe, which is reduced to water. Four more protons are pumped.
956: Cytochrome c oxidase: CuA, haem a, then the binuclear haem a3–CuB centre, where O₂ is reduced without releasing any toxic intermediate. 4 H⁺ are used to make water, 4 more are pumped. Inhibited by cyanide, azide and carbon monoxide.
